claims.claim: Politics is the process by which groups make collective decisions and allocate power and resources. OpenStax American Government 3e (section 1.1) defines politics as the process of gaining and exercising control within a government for the purpose of setting and achieving particular goals, especially those related to the division of resources within a nation; the American Political Science Association presents political science as the study of political processes and asks how power and resources are allocated in society.

Harold Lasswell's 1936 book 'Politics: Who Gets What, When, How' — whose title, in Britannica's words, later served as the standard lay definition of politics — frames politics as the allocation of valued things among people.
Political science is distinguished by its focus on power — the ability of one political actor to get another actor to do what it wants — at the international, national, and local levels.

Government is the means by which a society organizes itself and allocates authority in order to accomplish collective goals and provide benefits that the society as a whole needs (OpenStax American Government 3e, section 1.1). Politics differs from government as process differs from institution: politics is the activity of deciding what government does and who gets what.

Authority rests on legitimacy: following Max Weber, the basis of every system of authority, and of every kind of willingness to obey, is a belief — people obey because they believe the office or ruler has the right to command (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Political Legitimacy').

Coercion is power exercised through force or the threat of force without the target's acceptance; legitimacy — people's beliefs about political authority — is what distinguishes authority from mere coercion (SEP 'Political Legitimacy', Weber's descriptive account).
In the United States, government operates at multiple levels: the national (federal) government, state governments, and local governments (USA.gov, 'State and local governments').

The United Nations is an international organization founded in 1945, currently made up of 193 member states; the UN describes itself as the one place where the world's nations gather to discuss common problems and find shared solutions (United Nations, 'About Us').

Interpretive framing: politics is a neutral process — how groups settle disagreements and share things they cannot all have — so it is not inherently dirty; corruption is behavior that can appear inside politics, not the definition of it. Politics is how strangers govern themselves together.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is politics best understood as a neutral process of collective decision-making, or as a contest for power and advantage?
positions: OpenStax American Government 3e and APSA frame politics as the process by which groups make collective decisions and allocate power and resources — a neutral description of how societies choose and divide (OpenStax 1.1; APSA 'What is Political Science?').

Lasswell's 'who gets what, when, how' and Britannica's definition of power (one actor getting another to do what it wants) emphasize contest, distribution, and the capacity to shape others' behavior (Britannica, 'Harold Lasswell' and 'Political Science').
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the two as complementary rather than contradictory: politics is the process of collective decision-making, and the outcome of that process is always a distribution — who gets what, when, how. The lesson takes no position on whether any particular distribution is just or unjust, expresses no policy preferences, and uses only original fictional examples.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft in public/content/phase-4/lessons.json contained no definition of politics, no sources, no arenas, and no power/authority content. Its claims ('What Is Politics? is a foundational concept in Political Science & Government', 'a label on a toolbox drawer', 'Like reading a map legend before choosing a route') were generic boilerplate with no source support and were discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all boilerplate with source-verified content: working definition of politics (process of collective decision-making and allocation of power and resources) attributed to OpenStax American Government 3e 1.1 and APSA; Lasswell's 'who gets what, when, how' (1936) attributed via Britannica; the three arenas (local, national, international) each with an original example, grounded in Britannica, USA.gov, and the UN; power (ability to get another actor to do what it wants, Britannica) and authority vs coercion (legitimacy as belief, Weber via SEP); politics-as-process vs government-as-institution per OpenStax 1.1; the honest note (politics not inherently dirty) and the honest framing (how strangers govern themselves together) stated as interpretive claims. All examples are original and fictional.
rightsIssues: OpenStax American Government 3e is CC BY 4.0, but OpenStax's site states that automated/LLM ingestion requires prior written permission from OpenStax; therefore the source is classified REFERENCE_ONLY with aiIngestionAllowed false — facts were synthesized in original wording and no source prose was adapted. All other sources are treated as REFERENCE_ONLY; nothing is reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 1.1 What Is Government? — American Government 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor per the political-science source-map (openstax.org blocks direct automated fetch; read via Wayback Machine capture 20260203021607 of the canonical URL). New id minted — no American Government 3e records existed in the registries; the sociology subject's openstax-intro-sociology ids are a different book. Supports: the definition of politics as the process of gaining and exercising control within a government to set and achieve particular goals, especially dividing a nation's resources; politics as the process by which choices are made regarding how resources are allocated; the definition of government as the means by which a society organizes itself and allocates authority to accomplish collective goals and provide benefits; and the process-vs-institution contrast between politics and government. Facts synthesized in original wording; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: What is Political Science?
sourceRecords.notes: Fetched live 2026-08-22. Supports: political science as the study of governments, public policies, and political processes, systems, and behavior; the discipline's concern with how power and resources are allocated in society. Used, together with OpenStax 1.1, as the attribution for the lesson's working definition of politics (collective decisions; allocation of power and resources). Reference only; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Harold Lasswell
sourceRecords.notes: Britannica blocks direct fetch; read via Wayback Machine capture 20260526141120 of the canonical URL. Supports: Politics: Who Gets What, When, How (1936) and the fact that its title later served as the standard lay definition of politics; Lasswell's view of power as the ability to produce intended effects on people. Used for the one-line Lasswell attribution. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Political Science
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20260728225034 of the canonical URL (Britannica blocks direct fetch). Supports: the discipline's focus on power — defined as the ability of one political actor to get another actor to do what it wants — at the international, national, and local levels (the lesson's three arenas); the division of the field into domestic politics, comparative politics, and international relations. Reference only; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Political Legitimacy
sourceRecords.notes: Fetched live 2026-08-22. Supports: descriptive legitimacy as people's beliefs about political authority; Weber's account that the basis of every system of authority, and of every kind of willingness to obey, is a belief (Legitimitätsglaube); Weber's three sources of legitimacy (tradition, charisma, legality/rule of law); the contrast between authority grounded in belief and power exercised through coercion (section 2.2 Justifying Power and Coercion). Used for the power/authority and coercion/legitimacy distinction. Reference only.
